cards.explanation: The booklet lists genetic predisposition among non-modifiable risk factors.
cards.text: Inherited variants in {{c1::BRCA1/BRCA2}} are examples of genetic predisposition to breast cancer.
cards.question: Inherited variants in {{c1::BRCA1/BRCA2}} are examples of genetic predisposition to breast cancer.

cards.explanation: The source lists genes rather than detailing their molecular pathways.
cards.text: The additional predisposition gene listed with BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the risk table is {{c1::TP53}}.
cards.question: The additional predisposition gene listed with BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the risk table is {{c1::TP53}}.

cards.explanation: The background section associates atypical hyperplasia with subsequent cancer risk.
cards.text: Atypical {{c1::hyperplasia}} is a breast cancer risk factor identified in the booklet.
cards.question: Atypical {{c1::hyperplasia}} is a breast cancer risk factor identified in the booklet.

cards.explanation: The booklet identifies prolonged exposure as a breast cancer risk factor.
cards.text: Oestrogen exposure not balanced by progesterone is termed {{c1::unopposed oestrogen}} exposure.
cards.question: Oestrogen exposure not balanced by progesterone is termed {{c1::unopposed oestrogen}} exposure.

cards.explanation: The booklet links these alterations with abnormal proliferation; it does not specify detailed signalling pathways.
cards.text: Risk factors may promote breast tumourigenesis through genetic and {{c1::epigenetic}} alterations in breast epithelial cells.
cards.question: Risk factors may promote breast tumourigenesis through genetic and {{c1::epigenetic}} alterations in breast epithelial cells.

cards.explanation: The booklet labels IDC as the most common invasive carcinoma.
cards.text: Invasive ductal carcinoma is also described in the booklet as carcinoma of {{c1::no special type (NST)}}.
cards.question: Invasive ductal carcinoma is also described in the booklet as carcinoma of {{c1::no special type (NST)}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet names this subtype but provides no further histological diagnostic criteria.
cards.text: The alternative name given for mucinous breast carcinoma is {{c1::colloid carcinoma}}.
cards.question: The alternative name given for mucinous breast carcinoma is {{c1::colloid carcinoma}}.

cards.explanation: Size is considered alongside grade, nodal involvement and molecular profile.
cards.text: The physical extent measure listed among key breast cancer prognostic factors is {{c1::tumour size}}.
cards.question: The physical extent measure listed among key breast cancer prognostic factors is {{c1::tumour size}}.

cards.explanation: The practical includes a lymph node containing metastatic IDC.
cards.text: The spread-related prognostic factor listed alongside tumour size and grade is {{c1::nodal involvement}}.
cards.question: The spread-related prognostic factor listed alongside tumour size and grade is {{c1::nodal involvement}}.

cards.explanation: Grade and molecular profile inform prognosis and treatment together; the booklet does not give a numerical grading algorithm.
cards.text: The morphology-based prognostic factor listed in the booklet is {{c1::histological grade}}.
cards.question: The morphology-based prognostic factor listed in the booklet is {{c1::histological grade}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet gives tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors as examples.
cards.text: Breast cancers expressing ER and/or PR may respond to {{c1::endocrine therapy}}.
cards.question: Breast cancers expressing ER and/or PR may respond to {{c1::endocrine therapy}}.

cards.explanation: The source identifies it as a treatment example for hormone receptor-positive cancer.
cards.text: The named endocrine treatment listed alongside aromatase inhibitors is {{c1::tamoxifen}}.
cards.question: The named endocrine treatment listed alongside aromatase inhibitors is {{c1::tamoxifen}}.

cards.explanation: The accompanying diagram labels lobules, alveoli, ducts, nipple and areola.
cards.text: The labelled glandular units connected to breast ducts in Figure 1 are {{c1::lobules}}.
cards.question: The labelled glandular units connected to breast ducts in Figure 1 are {{c1::lobules}}.

cards.explanation: This is a direct label in Figure 1A.
cards.text: The channels labelled as connecting glandular tissue toward the nipple are the {{c1::ducts}}.
cards.question: The channels labelled as connecting glandular tissue toward the nipple are the {{c1::ducts}}.

cards.explanation: The figure distinguishes areola from nipple.
cards.text: The labelled pigmented region surrounding the nipple in Figure 1A is the {{c1::areola}}.
cards.question: The labelled pigmented region surrounding the nipple in Figure 1A is the {{c1::areola}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram places the myoepithelial layer outside the luminal epithelial layer.
cards.text: In the normal duct diagram, the inner cell layer is labelled {{c1::luminal epithelial cells}}.
cards.question: In the normal duct diagram, the inner cell layer is labelled {{c1::luminal epithelial cells}}.

cards.explanation: This peripheral layer provides the anatomical context for assessing an in situ lesion.
cards.text: The cell layer between the luminal epithelium and basement membrane in Figure 1A is the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.
cards.question: The cell layer between the luminal epithelium and basement membrane in Figure 1A is the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram shows a possible sequence toward carcinoma; it does not mean every hyperplastic lesion progresses.
cards.text: The increase in cell number illustrated before dysplasia in Figure 1B is labelled {{c1::hyperplasia}}.
cards.question: The increase in cell number illustrated before dysplasia in Figure 1B is labelled {{c1::hyperplasia}}.

cards.explanation: The invasive stage is illustrated with cells outside the duct boundary. Progression is schematic, not inevitable.
cards.text: The step separating in situ carcinoma from invasive carcinoma in Figure 1B is entry into the {{c1::surrounding stroma}}.
cards.question: The step separating in situ carcinoma from invasive carcinoma in Figure 1B is entry into the {{c1::surrounding stroma}}.

cards.explanation: DCIS is non-invasive: tumour cells remain within the ductal compartment.
cards.text: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is confined to the {{c1::ducts}} without invading the surrounding stroma.
cards.question: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is confined to the {{c1::ducts}} without invading the surrounding stroma.

cards.explanation: Breaching this boundary and entering the adjacent stroma defines invasive carcinoma.
cards.text: The boundary that remains unbreached in DCIS is the {{c1::basement membrane}}.
cards.question: The boundary that remains unbreached in DCIS is the {{c1::basement membrane}}.

cards.explanation: The handout uses preservation of this peripheral layer to distinguish DCIS from invasive disease.
cards.text: A preserved {{c1::myoepithelial cell layer}} around a breast lesion supports an in situ rather than invasive diagnosis.
cards.question: A preserved {{c1::myoepithelial cell layer}} around a breast lesion supports an in situ rather than invasive diagnosis.

cards.explanation: The source associates the comedo pattern with high grade and calcifications.
cards.text: DCIS with prominent central necrosis is described as {{c1::comedo}} DCIS.
cards.question: DCIS with prominent central necrosis is described as {{c1::comedo}} DCIS.

cards.explanation: The architectural clue is multiple rounded spaces within the tumour-cell sheet.
cards.text: The punched-out spaces within epithelial sheets in DCIS form a {{c1::cribriform}} pattern.
cards.question: The punched-out spaces within epithelial sheets in DCIS form a {{c1::cribriform}} pattern.

cards.explanation: The presence of supporting cores distinguishes papillary from micropapillary architecture.
cards.text: Papillary DCIS has {{c1::fibrovascular cores}} within its projections.
cards.question: Papillary DCIS has {{c1::fibrovascular cores}} within its projections.

cards.explanation: Micropapillary tufts lack the cores described in papillary DCIS.
cards.text: DCIS with cellular tufts lacking fibrovascular cores has a {{c1::micropapillary}} pattern.
cards.question: DCIS with cellular tufts lacking fibrovascular cores has a {{c1::micropapillary}} pattern.

cards.explanation: Solid refers to the architecture of the filled duct, rather than proving stromal invasion.
cards.text: When tumour cells completely fill the duct in DCIS, the pattern is {{c1::solid}}.
cards.question: When tumour cells completely fill the duct in DCIS, the pattern is {{c1::solid}}.

cards.explanation: The handout lists nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses and necrosis as grading features.
cards.text: The variation in nuclear size and shape assessed during DCIS grading is {{c1::nuclear pleomorphism}}.
cards.question: The variation in nuclear size and shape assessed during DCIS grading is {{c1::nuclear pleomorphism}}.

cards.explanation: Necrosis is also prominent in the comedo pattern. The source does not give numerical grading thresholds.
cards.text: The DCIS grading features listed alongside nuclear pleomorphism and mitoses include {{c1::necrosis}}.
cards.question: The DCIS grading features listed alongside nuclear pleomorphism and mitoses include {{c1::necrosis}}.

cards.explanation: These small calcifications can reveal an otherwise non-invasive ductal lesion.
cards.text: DCIS is often detected on mammography through {{c1::microcalcifications}}.
cards.question: DCIS is often detected on mammography through {{c1::microcalcifications}}.

cards.explanation: Non-obligate means progression is not inevitable. The booklet progression diagram is schematic, not a prediction for every LCIS lesion.
cards.text: LCIS is a breast cancer risk marker and a {{c1::non-obligate precursor}} to invasive cancer.
cards.question: LCIS is a breast cancer risk marker and a {{c1::non-obligate precursor}} to invasive cancer.

cards.explanation: The handout contrasts this presentation with palpable invasive ductal carcinoma.
cards.text: LCIS is usually found {{c1::incidentally}}, rather than presenting with a mass or calcification.
cards.question: LCIS is usually found {{c1::incidentally}}, rather than presenting with a mass or calcification.

cards.explanation: The lobular compartment remains enclosed; filling lobules does not itself demonstrate invasion.
cards.text: Small, uniform, dyscohesive tumour cells filling lobules are characteristic of {{c1::LCIS}}.
cards.question: Small, uniform, dyscohesive tumour cells filling lobules are characteristic of {{c1::LCIS}}.

cards.explanation: This is the defining in situ boundary; invasion requires tumour cells outside it.
cards.text: In LCIS, the {{c1::basement membrane}} remains intact.
cards.question: In LCIS, the {{c1::basement membrane}} remains intact.

cards.explanation: Its loss is an immunohistochemical clue to lobular differentiation.
cards.text: The adhesion marker typically lost in LCIS is {{c1::E-cadherin}}.
cards.question: The adhesion marker typically lost in LCIS is {{c1::E-cadherin}}.

cards.explanation: This is a typical profile described by the handout, not a universal rule.
cards.text: LCIS is often {{c1::ER/PR-positive}} and HER2-negative.
cards.question: LCIS is often {{c1::ER/PR-positive}} and HER2-negative.

cards.explanation: The source presents this as a possible risk-reduction strategy, not a mandatory treatment for every patient.
cards.text: A treatment that may be considered to reduce future breast cancer risk after LCIS is {{c1::hormonal therapy}}.
cards.question: A treatment that may be considered to reduce future breast cancer risk after LCIS is {{c1::hormonal therapy}}.

cards.explanation: The sources give an approximate frequency of 70–80%; the booklet also calls it carcinoma of no special type.
cards.text: The most common invasive breast carcinoma is {{c1::invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC)}}.
cards.question: The most common invasive breast carcinoma is {{c1::invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC)}}.

cards.explanation: The histological pattern contrasts with tumour confined to a duct and with single-file lobular infiltration.
cards.text: IDC often forms irregular nests or cords in {{c1::desmoplastic stroma}}.
cards.question: IDC often forms irregular nests or cords in {{c1::desmoplastic stroma}}.

cards.explanation: Interpret this as the typical distinction described in the handout, rather than an absolute rule.
cards.text: E-cadherin expression is typically {{c1::retained}} in IDC, unlike classic lobular carcinoma.
cards.question: E-cadherin expression is typically {{c1::retained}} in IDC, unlike classic lobular carcinoma.

cards.explanation: Invasive and in situ ductal components may coexist in the same specimen.
cards.text: An in situ lesion that may lie adjacent to IDC is {{c1::DCIS}}.
cards.question: An in situ lesion that may lie adjacent to IDC is {{c1::DCIS}}.

cards.explanation: The handout also describes necrosis and pleomorphism; the illustrated IDC shows invasive tumour nests and gland-like structures.
cards.text: A common architectural feature of IDC is formation of {{c1::glands}}.
cards.question: A common architectural feature of IDC is formation of {{c1::glands}}.

cards.explanation: Lobular morphology must be combined with location. E-cadherin loss can occur in both in situ and invasive lobular lesions.
cards.text: Small dyscohesive cells confined within lobules, with no basement-membrane breach, support {{c1::LCIS}} rather than ILC.
cards.question: Small dyscohesive cells confined within lobules, with no basement-membrane breach, support {{c1::LCIS}} rather than ILC.

cards.explanation: Papillary projections contain cores; micropapillary tufts do not.
cards.text: Papillary and micropapillary DCIS are separated morphologically by the presence or absence of {{c1::fibrovascular cores}}.
cards.question: Papillary and micropapillary DCIS are separated morphologically by the presence or absence of {{c1::fibrovascular cores}}.

cards.explanation: The source states that the mass is usually visible on mammography or ultrasound.
cards.text: IDC commonly presents clinically as a {{c1::palpable mass}}.
cards.question: IDC commonly presents clinically as a {{c1::palpable mass}}.

cards.explanation: IDC is listed as the most common invasive type.
cards.text: The second most common invasive breast carcinoma described in the handout is {{c1::invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC)}}.
cards.question: The second most common invasive breast carcinoma described in the handout is {{c1::invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC)}}.

cards.explanation: Loss of this adhesion marker helps explain the dispersed growth pattern.
cards.text: The dyscohesion of classic ILC cells is associated with loss of {{c1::E-cadherin}}.
cards.question: The dyscohesion of classic ILC cells is associated with loss of {{c1::E-cadherin}}.

cards.explanation: Individual dyscohesive tumour cells infiltrate through the stroma in lines.
cards.text: The classic infiltrative growth pattern in ILC is {{c1::single-file}} infiltration.
cards.question: The classic infiltrative growth pattern in ILC is {{c1::single-file}} infiltration.

cards.explanation: The source describes this as an additional lobular growth pattern.
cards.text: ILC cells arranged around ducts or lobules form a {{c1::targetoid}} pattern.
cards.question: ILC cells arranged around ducts or lobules form a {{c1::targetoid}} pattern.

cards.explanation: The handout also highlights multifocal disease. These are tendencies, not requirements.
cards.text: ILC may affect both breasts; this distribution is called {{c1::bilateral}} disease.
cards.question: ILC may affect both breasts; this distribution is called {{c1::bilateral}} disease.

cards.explanation: Multifocal describes multiple foci; it is distinct from bilateral involvement.
cards.text: Several separate tumour foci within a breast constitute {{c1::multifocal}} disease, a distribution associated with ILC.
cards.question: Several separate tumour foci within a breast constitute {{c1::multifocal}} disease, a distribution associated with ILC.

cards.explanation: ILC may be difficult to detect on mammography. The statement compares modalities in the lecture context.
cards.text: For ILC, the handout describes {{c1::MRI}} as more sensitive than mammography.
cards.question: For ILC, the handout describes {{c1::MRI}} as more sensitive than mammography.

cards.explanation: The source notes that a Luminal A profile is common, without claiming that all ILC has that profile.
cards.text: ILC is usually {{c1::ER/PR-positive}} and HER2-negative.
cards.question: ILC is usually {{c1::ER/PR-positive}} and HER2-negative.

cards.explanation: Haematoxylin and eosin staining shows tissue morphology; it does not establish receptor status.
cards.text: The routine stain used to assess breast tumour architecture and invasion is {{c1::H&E}}.
cards.question: The routine stain used to assess breast tumour architecture and invasion is {{c1::H&E}}.

cards.explanation: The handout lists ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 among the markers assessed using IHC.
cards.text: Breast tumour receptor status requires {{c1::immunohistochemistry (IHC)}} rather than H&E morphology alone.
cards.question: Breast tumour receptor status requires {{c1::immunohistochemistry (IHC)}} rather than H&E morphology alone.

cards.explanation: The key comparison is location relative to the basement membrane.
cards.text: On H&E, tumour cells within surrounding stroma rather than confined within a duct indicate {{c1::invasion}}.
cards.question: On H&E, tumour cells within surrounding stroma rather than confined within a duct indicate {{c1::invasion}}.

cards.explanation: The handout lists mitoses alongside pleomorphism, grade and necrosis.
cards.text: The division figures assessed on H&E when examining tumour cytology are {{c1::mitoses}}.
cards.question: The division figures assessed on H&E when examining tumour cytology are {{c1::mitoses}}.

cards.explanation: This receptor profile helps guide endocrine treatment decisions.
cards.text: ER and PR immunostaining assesses {{c1::hormone receptor status}} in breast cancer.
cards.question: ER and PR immunostaining assesses {{c1::hormone receptor status}} in breast cancer.

cards.explanation: The source links HER2 overexpression with targeted therapy.
cards.text: The breast cancer marker targeted by trastuzumab is {{c1::HER2}}.
cards.question: The breast cancer marker targeted by trastuzumab is {{c1::HER2}}.

cards.explanation: The handout uses lower versus higher proliferation to help distinguish Luminal A and Luminal B profiles.
cards.text: The marker used as a breast tumour proliferation index is {{c1::Ki-67}}.
cards.question: The marker used as a breast tumour proliferation index is {{c1::Ki-67}}.

cards.explanation: Demonstrating this layer supports an in situ lesion; the result is interpreted with morphology.
cards.text: p63, SMA and calponin are markers used to identify the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.
cards.question: p63, SMA and calponin are markers used to identify the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.

cards.explanation: The handout also describes HER2 negativity and low Ki-67.
cards.text: The typical hormone receptor profile of Luminal A breast cancer is {{c1::ER-positive and PR-positive}}.
cards.question: The typical hormone receptor profile of Luminal A breast cancer is {{c1::ER-positive and PR-positive}}.

cards.explanation: This is the simplified receptor-based profile presented in the source.
cards.text: In the handout, Luminal A breast cancer is {{c1::HER2-negative}}.
cards.question: In the handout, Luminal A breast cancer is {{c1::HER2-negative}}.

cards.explanation: Ki-67 reflects proliferation. The handout supplies no percentage cut-offs.
cards.text: Compared with Luminal B, Luminal A usually has {{c1::lower Ki-67}}.
cards.question: Compared with Luminal B, Luminal A usually has {{c1::lower Ki-67}}.

cards.explanation: The source associates this profile with a relatively good prognosis.
cards.text: The therapy class associated with the hormone receptor-positive Luminal A profile is {{c1::hormonal (endocrine) therapy}}.
cards.question: The therapy class associated with the hormone receptor-positive Luminal A profile is {{c1::hormonal (endocrine) therapy}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses PR± and HER2±, so HER2 positivity is not required for Luminal B.
cards.text: Luminal B breast cancer is ER-positive, while its PR and HER2 status may be {{c1::variable}}.
cards.question: Luminal B breast cancer is ER-positive, while its PR and HER2 status may be {{c1::variable}}.

cards.explanation: The handout associates Luminal B with higher Ki-67. This is a subtype-level tendency, not an individual outcome prediction.
cards.text: In the source comparison, Luminal B is {{c1::more aggressive}} than Luminal A.
cards.question: In the source comparison, Luminal B is {{c1::more aggressive}} than Luminal A.

cards.explanation: This is the handout’s receptor-based teaching shorthand; receptor testing alone does not define every intrinsic molecular subtype.
cards.text: The simplified HER2-enriched profile in the handout is ER-negative, PR-negative and {{c1::HER2-positive}}.
cards.question: The simplified HER2-enriched profile in the handout is ER-negative, PR-negative and {{c1::HER2-positive}}.

cards.explanation: The handout also associates it with a poorer prognosis; neither claim guarantees an individual patient’s response.
cards.text: The treatment sensitivity highlighted for triple-negative breast cancer in the handout is sensitivity to {{c1::chemotherapy}}.
cards.question: The treatment sensitivity highlighted for triple-negative breast cancer in the handout is sensitivity to {{c1::chemotherapy}}.

cards.explanation: LCIS and ILC both typically lose E-cadherin. The invasive distinction still depends on cells breaching the boundary and entering stroma.
cards.text: E-cadherin loss supports lobular differentiation but cannot, by itself, establish {{c1::invasion}}.
cards.question: E-cadherin loss supports lobular differentiation but cannot, by itself, establish {{c1::invasion}}.

cards.explanation: Morphology shows architecture and invasion, whereas marker staining provides ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 information.
cards.text: If H&E establishes carcinoma but treatment depends on receptor status, the additional technique required is {{c1::IHC}}.
cards.question: If H&E establishes carcinoma but treatment depends on receptor status, the additional technique required is {{c1::IHC}}.

cards.explanation: This applies the simplified teaching profile. The source gives no Ki-67 cut-off or full molecular-testing algorithm.
cards.text: A hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumour with low proliferation fits the handout’s {{c1::Luminal A}} profile.
cards.question: A hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumour with low proliferation fits the handout’s {{c1::Luminal A}} profile.

cards.explanation: Classify using all three results. The basal-like molecular category is related but not identical.
cards.text: A tumour negative for ER, PR and HER2 has a {{c1::triple-negative}} receptor profile.
cards.question: A tumour negative for ER, PR and HER2 has a {{c1::triple-negative}} receptor profile.

cards.explanation: The practical lists a lymph node containing metastatic IDC, but provides no labelled lymph-node micrograph to interpret.
cards.text: IDC found within a lymph node represents {{c1::metastatic disease}} rather than an in situ breast lesion.
cards.question: IDC found within a lymph node represents {{c1::metastatic disease}} rather than an in situ breast lesion.

cards.explanation: The normal H&E illustration distinguishes stroma, adipose tissue, ducts and lobules.
cards.text: The labelled supportive tissue between breast structures in Figure 3 is {{c1::connective tissue (stroma)}}.
cards.question: The labelled supportive tissue between breast structures in Figure 3 is {{c1::connective tissue (stroma)}}.

cards.explanation: The identification is grounded in the figure’s label.
cards.text: The pale, large-cell tissue labelled in Figure 3 is {{c1::adipose tissue}}.
cards.question: The pale, large-cell tissue labelled in Figure 3 is {{c1::adipose tissue}}.

cards.explanation: Combine the compartment, preserved peripheral layer and lack of invasion; atypical cells alone do not establish invasion.
cards.text: A lesion fills a duct, has a preserved myoepithelial rim and has no stromal infiltration. These findings support {{c1::DCIS}} rather than IDC.
cards.question: A lesion fills a duct, has a preserved myoepithelial rim and has no stromal infiltration. These findings support {{c1::DCIS}} rather than IDC.

cards.explanation: The practical asks you to identify the boundary breach, rather than relying on pleomorphism alone.
cards.text: For a ductal lesion, finding tumour cells beyond the duct boundary in surrounding stroma changes the classification to {{c1::invasive carcinoma}}.
cards.question: For a ductal lesion, finding tumour cells beyond the duct boundary in surrounding stroma changes the classification to {{c1::invasive carcinoma}}.

cards.explanation: The instructions start with low power before selecting a region for higher magnification.
cards.text: Begin locating a specimen with the {{c1::low-power objective}}.
cards.question: Begin locating a specimen with the {{c1::low-power objective}}.

cards.explanation: Compare the cohesive nests in the ductal example with dispersed lobular infiltration.
cards.text: Irregular cohesive tumour nests in desmoplastic stroma favour {{c1::IDC}} over classic ILC.
cards.question: Irregular cohesive tumour nests in desmoplastic stroma favour {{c1::IDC}} over classic ILC.

cards.explanation: Combine the infiltrative location with the characteristic lobular growth pattern.
cards.text: Single-file dyscohesive tumour cells infiltrating breast stroma favour {{c1::ILC}} over DCIS.
cards.question: Single-file dyscohesive tumour cells infiltrating breast stroma favour {{c1::ILC}} over DCIS.

cards.explanation: This makes the desired area easier to retain in the smaller high-power field.
cards.text: Before changing to high power, {{c1::centre the area of interest}} using the stage controls.
cards.question: Before changing to high power, {{c1::centre the area of interest}} using the stage controls.

cards.explanation: The booklet explains that only small focusing corrections should then be needed.
cards.text: Objectives that stay approximately in focus when switched after low-power focusing are called {{c1::parfocal}}.
cards.question: Objectives that stay approximately in focus when switched after low-power focusing are called {{c1::parfocal}}.

cards.explanation: The procedure explicitly switches to fine adjustment at high power.
cards.text: Once the high-power objective is selected, use the {{c1::fine focus only}} to adjust focus.
cards.question: Once the high-power objective is selected, use the {{c1::fine focus only}} to adjust focus.

cards.explanation: The booklet instructs repeating the selection, centring and high-power steps.
cards.text: If the specimen cannot be found at high power, return to {{c1::low power}} and re-centre it.
cards.question: If the specimen cannot be found at high power, return to {{c1::low power}} and re-centre it.

cards.explanation: The instructions also adjust the condenser for even illumination.
cards.text: The {{c1::iris diaphragm}} is adjusted to optimise contrast and resolution.
cards.question: The {{c1::iris diaphragm}} is adjusted to optimise contrast and resolution.

cards.explanation: Focus the right-eye image first, then adjust the left-eye diopter without disturbing the fine-focus control.
cards.text: Different focusing needs between the eyes are adjusted with the eyepiece {{c1::diopter ring}}.
cards.question: Different focusing needs between the eyes are adjusted with the eyepiece {{c1::diopter ring}}.

cards.explanation: This follows the stated microscope procedure. At high power, the instructions specify fine focus only.
cards.text: During initial low-power coarse focusing, the booklet instructs moving the objective {{c1::away from the specimen}} until it comes into focus.
cards.question: During initial low-power coarse focusing, the booklet instructs moving the objective {{c1::away from the specimen}} until it comes into focus.

Papillary and micropapillary DCIS are separated morphologically by the presence or absence of {{c1::fibrovascular cores}}.

IDC commonly presents clinically as a {{c1::palpable mass}}.
The second most common invasive breast carcinoma described in the handout is {{c1::invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC)}}.
The dyscohesion of classic ILC cells is associated with loss of {{c1::E-cadherin}}.
The classic infiltrative growth pattern in ILC is {{c1::single-file}} infiltration.
ILC cells arranged around ducts or lobules form a {{c1::targetoid}} pattern.
ILC may affect both breasts; this distribution is called {{c1::bilateral}} disease.
Several separate tumour foci within a breast constitute {{c1::multifocal}} disease, a distribution associated with ILC.
For ILC, the handout describes {{c1::MRI}} as more sensitive than mammography.
ILC is usually {{c1::ER/PR-positive}} and HER2-negative.
The routine stain used to assess breast tumour architecture and invasion is {{c1::H&E}}.
Breast tumour receptor status requires {{c1::immunohistochemistry (IHC)}} rather than H&E morphology alone.
On H&E, tumour cells within surrounding stroma rather than confined within a duct indicate {{c1::invasion}}.
The division figures assessed on H&E when examining tumour cytology are {{c1::mitoses}}.
ER and PR immunostaining assesses {{c1::hormone receptor status}} in breast cancer.
The breast cancer marker targeted by trastuzumab is {{c1::HER2}}.
The marker used as a breast tumour proliferation index is {{c1::Ki-67}}.
p63, SMA and calponin are markers used to identify the {{c1::myoepithelial layer}}.
The typical hormone receptor profile of Luminal A breast cancer is {{c1::ER-positive and PR-positive}}.
In the handout, Luminal A breast cancer is {{c1::HER2-negative}}.
Compared with Luminal B, Luminal A usually has {{c1::lower Ki-67}}.
The therapy class associated with the hormone receptor-positive Luminal A profile is {{c1::hormonal (endocrine) therapy}}.
Luminal B breast cancer is ER-positive, while its PR and HER2 status may be {{c1::variable}}.
In the source comparison, Luminal B is {{c1::more aggressive}} than Luminal A.
The simplified HER2-enriched profile in the handout is ER-negative, PR-negative and {{c1::HER2-positive}}.
The treatment sensitivity highlighted for triple-negative breast cancer in the handout is sensitivity to {{c1::chemotherapy}}.
E-cadherin loss supports lobular differentiation but cannot, by itself, establish {{c1::invasion}}.
If H&E establishes carcinoma but treatment depends on receptor status, the additional technique required is {{c1::IHC}}.
A hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumour with low proliferation fits the handout’s {{c1::Luminal A}} profile.
A tumour negative for ER, PR and HER2 has a {{c1::triple-negative}} receptor profile.
IDC found within a lymph node represents {{c1::metastatic disease}} rather than an in situ breast lesion.

The labelled supportive tissue between breast structures in Figure 3 is {{c1::connective tissue (stroma)}}.
The pale, large-cell tissue labelled in Figure 3 is {{c1::adipose tissue}}.
A lesion fills a duct, has a preserved myoepithelial rim and has no stromal infiltration. These findings support {{c1::DCIS}} rather than IDC.
For a ductal lesion, finding tumour cells beyond the duct boundary in surrounding stroma changes the classification to {{c1::invasive carcinoma}}.

Begin locating a specimen with the {{c1::low-power objective}}.
Irregular cohesive tumour nests in desmoplastic stroma favour {{c1::IDC}} over classic ILC.
Single-file dyscohesive tumour cells infiltrating breast stroma favour {{c1::ILC}} over DCIS.

Before changing to high power, {{c1::centre the area of interest}} using the stage controls.
Objectives that stay approximately in focus when switched after low-power focusing are called {{c1::parfocal}}.
Once the high-power objective is selected, use the {{c1::fine focus only}} to adjust focus.
If the specimen cannot be found at high power, return to {{c1::low power}} and re-centre it.
The {{c1::iris diaphragm}} is adjusted to optimise contrast and resolution.
Different focusing needs between the eyes are adjusted with the eyepiece {{c1::diopter ring}}.
During initial low-power coarse focusing, the booklet instructs moving the objective {{c1::away from the specimen}} until it comes into focus.
